title: The Bell of Dhammazedi
subtitle: Yangon, Myanmar · 1608
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Muted documentary still, the wide muddy tidal river at Yangon in Lower Burma, early seventeenth century, brown-gold water and low green banks under warm humid haze with soft pale light and old-bronze glints, quiet melancholy and uncanny, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. beats.vo: A giant bell has been lost in a river for four centuries. Cast in fourteen eighty-four for Myanmar's Shwedagon Pagoda, it was said to be the largest bell ever made.

facts.claim: The bell was cast in 1484 by order of King Dhammazedi (Mon ruler of Hanthawaddy/Bago) and presented to the Shwedagon Pagoda in Dagon, today's Yangon, Myanmar ('Cast in fourteen eighty-four for Myanmar's Shwedagon Pagoda'). Wikipedia: cast 5 February 1484; DVB 2014: commissioned 1484; Malorie's Adventures (Oct 2026): cast 1484, hung at Shwedagon. Fox/AP gives only 'late 15th century'; one source says 1490, so only the year 1484 (majority) is used.

Said to be the largest bell ever made ('giant bell', 'said to be the largest bell ever made'): Wikipedia List of heaviest bells: 'the largest bell to have existed in recorded history'; DVB: 'reputedly the world's largest bell'; Fox/AP headline: 'the world's largest bell'. Weight left out of VO deliberately: sources give 270 t (DVB, Fox/AP), 294 t (Wikipedia, from 180,000 viss) and 'nearly 300 tonnes' (Nation).

In 1608 the Portuguese mercenary Filipe de Brito e Nicote (ruler of Syriam/Thanlyin) had the bell taken from the Shwedagon to be melted down and made into cannons ('seized it, to melt down for cannons'). Wikipedia: de Brito and his men took it, to be 'melted down and made into cannons'; DVB: 'Portuguese warlord and mercenary', 1608, wanted it melted down to make cannons; Fox/AP: 'Portuguese mercenary Philip de Brito', to be melted down and made into cannons; Malorie's Adventures: 1608, needed metal for cannons. (Wikipedia: his men rolled it down the hill onto a raft; elephants hauled it.)

It sank where the Yangon and Bago rivers meet, the vessel carrying it going down under the weight. Wikipedia: at the confluence of the Bago and Yangon rivers off Monkey Point the raft broke up, 'the load proved too heavy'; DVB: sank under its own weight while transported by boat, at the confluence of the Pegu (Bago) and Rangoon (Yangon) rivers; Fox/AP: a 'rickety vessel' sank under the weight where the Yangon and Bago rivers meet Pazundaung Creek; Malorie's: confluence of the Bago and Yangon rivers. Sources disagree raft vs boat, so the VO says 'the vessel carrying it'. Claim that it also dragged down de Brito's flagship (Wikipedia, Malorie's) left out.

Divers have searched for decades ('Divers have searched for decades'): DVB 2014: earlier attempts since the 1980s failed; Nation (Sep 2014): searches in 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2014; Wikipedia: 2000 Hatcher plan, 115 sonar dives, 2010 Damien Lay survey, 2014 search.

In 2014 a team claimed to have found it; nothing was raised ('In twenty fourteen, a team claimed to have found it. Nothing was raised.'). Wikipedia: in August 2014 San Linn claimed the bell had been found, 'these claims were found to be false, and searches for the bell continue'; Nation (15 Sep 2014): dive-team leader confirmed his team never found the bell, only a shipwreck, info officer: 'the bell has not been discovered yet'; Malorie's (Oct 2026): the expedition found only old barges and unrelated wreckage. Searcher named only in facts, not in VO.

It may lie beneath deep mud ('It may lie beneath deep mud'): Wikipedia: may be buried under up to 25 ft (7.6 m) of mud; DVB 2014: silt layers make recovery very difficult; other accounts: some 8 m of sediment. Kept as 'may'.

Still unsolved as of Nov 2026: Malorie's Adventures (dated 16 Oct 2026): 'sank in 1608 and nobody has found it since', nothing recovered; Wikipedia (Great Bell of Dhammazedi, current): has not been found, searches continue; Wikipedia List of heaviest bells (current): 'remains buried to this day', disqualified until recovered. Searches for 2024-2026 news found no recovery or confirmed find; the only 'found' claim (Aug 2014) was not substantiated.
